title: Trump Accuses His Own Government of Falsifying Economic Data
excerpt: In his Thanksgiving message on social media, Trump called for an investigation into a routine revision to economic data, calling it a “massive, and purposeful, error.”
content_html:
“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late,” Trump posted on Truth Social Thursday. “A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated.” His holiday post also made jabs at the “Radical Far Left,” immigrants, and “Reporters and Citizens” who have criticized his White House ballroom project.

On Wednesday, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) revised its estimate of third-quarter annualised growth to 4.3%, up from the advance estimate of 3.4% published on Oct. 29. Annualized growth tracks how much the economy would grow over a year if it kept growing at that quarter’s pace. The updated figures, which were published according to a prescheduled calendar, reflect an increase from 2.2% in the second quarter.

In another post on Thursday, Trump called the revision a “massive, and purposeful, error.”

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” he posted. He did not provide evidence of manipulation.

TIME has reached out to the Commerce Department and BEA for comment.

It’s not the first time that Trump has sought to undermine economic data that didn’t reflect his claims of economic prosperity. In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump frequently claimed the U.S. economy was experiencing a major boom, citing stock market highs and pointing to his tariffs as enriching the country. When the advance estimate was published in October, the White House called it “the strongest pace in a year” and evidence of “an economy that continues to outperform the so-called ‘experts.’” Voters, however, appeared to see things differently: 76% said economic conditions were “not so good” or “poor,” according to the AP Voter Poll, and two-thirds said they believed Trump’s policies had driven up inflation. Nine in 10 midterm voters said the cost of living was a major factor in their vote.

Reports on Wednesday showed a mixed picture of the economy. The BEA raised its estimate of growth in consumer spending and private fixed investment combined, pointing to stronger economic growth in the third quarter. At the same time, a separate BEA report showed that the personal consumption expenditures price index, a key measure of inflation, rose 3.8% in October from a year earlier. New York Fed analysts also estimated last month that Trump’s tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to year-over-year inflation for consumer goods by February. Without tariffs, the researchers said, goods prices would have fallen slightly.

Trump’s history of selectively undermining economic data

Even before he became President, Trump questioned the integrity of economic statistics. “It’s a false economy that we’re living in,” Trump, who was then the GOP frontrunner, told CBS’ Face the Nation in 2015, before launching into a diatribe against the unemployment rate. 

On the campaign trail, he called the job numbers “phony” and a “joke.” In February 2016, he falsely stated the unemployment rate was as high as 35% and that he “heard” it even reached 42%, while official figures showed the figure hovered near 5%. Later that year, without evidence, he called the 5% unemployment rate “one of the biggest hoaxes in modern politics.”

But after his first inauguration, Trump slightly changed his tune on economic figures. In March 2017, then-Press Secretary Sean Spicer was asked about a released jobs report, to which he responded: “I talked to the President prior to this, and he said to quote him very clearly — ‘They may have been phony in the past, but it’s very real now.’” At a round table in July that year, Trump acknowledged having dismissed unemployment figures before, adding: “now I accept those numbers very proudly.”

The President has also accused the U.S. press, without evidence, of manipulating some figures to deny his achievements. In 2019, Trump accused the press of revising a 3.1% economic growth figure downward to 2.9%, when reporters were citing figures from Trump’s own Commerce Department.

In July 2022, while out of office and speaking in Arizona, Trump slammed a 40-year record-high inflation rate of 9.1% under the Joe Biden Administration, and he claimed, without substantiation, that the actual number was much higher. “Biden created the worst inflation in 47 years,” Trump said.

In August 2024, the Biden Administration’s Bureau of Labor Statistics preliminarily revised down the benchmark payroll growth for the year ending in March by 818,000 jobs. Trump called it a “massive scandal,” arguing that it wasn’t a revision but “a total lie,” and accused the Biden Administration of “fraudulently manipulating job statistics to hide the true extent of the economic ruin that they’ve inflicted on America.” 

In August 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, he fired BLS commissioner Erika McEntarfer, a Biden appointee, for allegedly manipulating job figures to reflect poorly on his Administration. “Today’s Jobs Numbers were RIGGED to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad,” the President posted on Truth Social at the time. The White House also published what it said was a “lengthy history of inaccuracies and incompetence,” citing revisions.

Trump’s own former BLS commissioner William Beach and other federal statistical experts have said claims of manipulation have no merit and undermine the credibility of economic statistics. 

How the numbers are calculated—and revised

The BEA routinely revises its estimates of annualized growth and other economic data. The agency bases its advance estimate on two or three months of available source data and makes assumptions where data is still missing or preliminary. When new data or survey results become available, the agency revises its figures to be more accurate.

Those updates happen on a prescheduled basis. The advance estimate typically comes out around a month after the quarter ends, the second estimate about two months after, and the third estimate around three months after. For the third quarter of 2026, the BEA released the advance estimate on Oct. 29 and the second estimate Nov. 25, with the third scheduled for Dec. 23. The White House budget office published the calendar for all three estimates in September 2025. While federal policy allows for schedule changes in certain circumstances, such as the 2025 government shutdown, in this case, contrary to Trump’s assertion that the second estimate was “three weeks late,” the estimates came out on time.

Wednesday’s revision happened because revised software price and retail sales data pushed up estimates of software investment and goods spending, while new Census survey data lowered the estimate of health care spending, the agency said. The agency cited new and revised Energy Department data for consumer spending on gas as pushing up overall goods spending. The 0.9-percentage-point revision was bigger than the BEA’s historical average of 0.5 percentage points difference between a first and second estimate.

There are broader pressures that can make early economic estimates less precise. A Nov. 17 report from the American Statistical Association (ASA) found that response rates declined from 2016 to 2025 in eight of the 10 surveys of businesses and prices it reviewed. Fewer responses can reduce precision and force agencies to rely more heavily on estimates for missing data. Falling participation can also lead to bias based on which households or businesses respond and which don’t. Brookings analysts suggested in April that people may be difficult to contact, reluctant to respond because they are busy, or concerned about keeping their data private.

“A falling response rate does not automatically mean that a survey’s estimates are inaccurate. It increases the risk that estimates do not remain as accurate and representative as they have been in the past,” the ASA said.

The BEA has also faced staffing cuts under the Trump Administration. Its workforce shrank by around 21% from 473 employees at the end of fiscal 2024 to 374 by July 2026, according to federal personnel data compiled by the ASA. The ASA also found that the BEA’s fiscal 2026 budget fell around 8% from the previous year after adjusting for inflation. The association warned that staffing losses and funding constraints threaten the timeliness, quality, and availability of federal statistics.

The agency, however, did not name these pressures in its explanation for Wednesday’s revision.

Without responding to Trump’s allegation of purposeful error, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick praised the BEA’s revised estimate as evidence that “The American Economy under The Trump Administration is doing BETTER than every expert estimated!”

“This Thanksgiving, I am thankful to be a part of President Trump's administration, not only for the extraordinary honor of serving the American people, but because I love this Country so much, I know how much better off we are today than we were two years ago, and I know the incredible heights we can reach in the years ahead,” Lutnick posted on X. “4.3% Growth—Happy Thanksgiving!!”

blocks.html_en: “This Thanksgiving, I am thankful to be a part of President Trump's administration, not only for the extraordinary honor of serving the American people, but because I love this Country so much, I know how much better off we are today than we were two years ago, and I know the incredible heights we can reach in the years ahead,” Lutnick posted on X. “4.3% Growth—Happy Thanksgiving!!”
